episodes.title: An 86-minute guide to finding PMF | Rob Snyder (Author, The Power of Pull)
episodes.description:
Rob Snyder is the author of The Power of Pull and writes the newsletter The Physics of Startups. He has advised more than 50 startups on growing from zero to $1 million in ARR, drawing on his own experience as a founder who spent two years pushing a product the market didn’t want before accidentally stumbling onto what actually works. In this episode, we walk step by step through his framework for finding product-market fit, from coming up with an idea to closing your first handful of deals.
We discuss:
1. The PULL framework: Project, Unavoidable, List of options, Limitations
2. Where the best startup ideas come from
3. Tactics for cold outreach and running your first sales call
4. Why Rob advises against design partners
5. Goblin mode: what to do when nothing is working
6. How to apply the PULL framework inside larger companies
episodes.descriptionCN:
罗布·斯奈德 (Rob Snyder) 是《拉力的力量》一书的作者，也是时事通讯《初创公司的物理学》的作者。他利用自己作为创始人的经验，为 50 多家初创公司提供了从零到 100 万美元的 ARR 增长建议，他花了两年时间推出市场不想要的产品，然后意外地发现了真正有效的产品。在本集中，我们将逐步介绍他寻找产品与市场契合度的框架，从提出想法到完成第一笔交易。
我们讨论：
1. PULL 框架：项目、不可避免的问题、选项列表、限制
2. 最好的创业创意来自哪里
3. 冷外展和第一次销售拜访的策略
4. 为什么 Rob 不建议设计合作伙伴
5.妖精模式：什么都不起作用时该怎么办
6. 如何在大公司内部应用PULL框架

episodes.title: Inside the black box of AI: How AI models actually think | Emmanuel Ameisen (Anthropic)
episodes.description:
Emmanuel Ameisen is an interpretability researcher at Anthropic, where he looks inside LLMs like Claude to understand how they think. Before joining Anthropic, he spent years in applied ML at Stripe and Insight, and is the author of Building Machine Learning Powered Applications. His research has produced some of the most striking findings in the field: that models form general representations of concepts, plan many tokens ahead without stating those plans explicitly, and may exhibit something structurally similar to the distinction between conscious and unconscious processing in humans.
We discuss:
1. Why the “next-token predictor” framing undersells how models actually plan and think
2. Why anthropomorphizing AI can actually be the right approach
3. Why models are “grown,” not built
4. What the “J space” reveals about model self-awareness
5. The smooth scaling curve behind what look like sudden capability jumps
6. How interpretability connects to AI alignment and safety
episodes.descriptionCN:
Emmanuel Ameisen 是 Anthropic 的可解释性研究员，他深入研究像 Claude 这样的法学硕士，以了解他们的想法。在加入 Anthropic 之前，他在 Stripe 和 Insight 从事应用机器学习工作多年，并且是《构建机器学习驱动的应用程序》一书的作者。他的研究产生了该领域一些最引人注目的发现：模型形成概念的一般表示，提前计划许多标记而无需明确说明这些计划，并且可能在结构上表现出类似于人类有意识和无意识处理之间的区别的东西。
我们讨论：
1. 为什么“下一个令牌预测器”框架低估了模型实际计划和思考的方式
2. 为什么人工智能拟人化实际上是正确的方法
3. 为什么模型是“成长”的，而不是构建的
4.“J空间”揭示了模特的自我意识
5.看似突然的能力跳跃背后的平滑缩放曲线
6. 可解释性如何与人工智能一致性和安全性联系起来

episodes.title: Why every company now needs to think and operate like a lab team | Josh Woodward (Google Labs, Gemini, AI Studio)
episodes.description:
Josh Woodward is the head of Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio. He has spent over 17 years at Google and oversees its longest-running and largest labs team, whose products include NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook), Project Genie, and Flow. His job is to find, experiment with, and scale new AI products, and he has built one of the most distinctive product cultures in the industry for generating ideas, running experiments, and, even more importantly, knowing when to quit.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why every company now needs to think and operate like a labs team
2. Where the best ideas really come from
3. The “almost possible” framework
4. How to recognize genuine product-market fit early
5. When to kill an idea
6. What skills are rising in value in the AI era
7. Why roles are not actually blurring into one universal builder role
8. How to set up your internal labs team

episodes.title: OpenAI’s Head of ChatGPT: We’re entering a new era of AI (again) | Tibo Sottiaux
episodes.description:
Tibo Sottiaux leads ChatGPT and Codex at OpenAI. Under his stewardship, OpenAI has shipped some of its most consequential consumer launches: Codex, ChatGPT Work, and most recently, the new Dots personal agent platform. He joined me at DevDay, hours after his team launched more than 20 new products, to talk about where things are heading.
We discuss:
1. Dots, OpenAI’s new personal AI assistant
2. Why most actions on the internet will soon be taken by agents
3. Why loops, graphs, and fine-tuning agent workflows are a passing phase
4. Which skills are trending up and down in the AI era
5. How Tibo’s Dot warned him about a production outage five minutes before the launch
6. OpenAI’s approach to AI safety

episodes.title: The grief, loneliness, and burnout sweeping through the tech industry right now | Molly Graham
episodes.description:
Molly Graham is back for round two, and this one is even more powerful. Molly has spent more than 20 years helping organizations and the humans inside them navigate growth and change. She’s held leadership roles at Google, Facebook, Quip, and the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and is the host of TED’s WorkLife podcast (which she took over from Adam Grant). She also runs Glue Club, a leadership community for senior operators, and writes a popular newsletter called Lessons.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why Molly’s famous “give away your Legos” career advice no longer holds true in an AI world
2. The grief, loneliness, and burnout sweeping through the tech industry right now
3. Why delegating to AI is fundamentally different from delegating to a human
4. The fear narrative around AI job displacement, and why it’s overblown
5. Which Legos you should never give to AI
6. What the best managers are doing right now

在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：

episodes.title: 90 minutes of unfiltered product advice from Snap and Discord’s product chief | Peter Sellis
episodes.description:
Peter Sellis was the first product manager at Snapchat, where he spent seven years building one of the most beloved consumer products in history. He went on to serve as Head of Product at Discord, where he helped drive some of the fastest user growth the platform had seen. Having left his role at Discord, he gets to be especially real and unfiltered — nothing to promote, no PR, no comms team.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why Peter designs teams like . . . terrorist organizations
2. What it was really like to manage Nikita Bier
3. Why the median PM is so bad
4. Why Snapchat’s ads business never reached its potential
5. Why growth almost always comes from the core product
6. Peter’s three “oxymorons” of great product management

episodes.title: How Anthropic ships the #1 LLM in the World — with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang
episodes.description:
An agent’s sandbox can die without taking the whole agent with it. That’s the idea behind “the brain and the hands,” Anthropic’s architecture for Claude Managed Agents.
Now that the dust has settled on Opus 5.5, it is universally agreed to be the best model in the world. In this conversation with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang, Anthropic’s Heads of Engineering and of Product, goes inside the systems that turn model capabilities into products developers can use.
We cover:
- Why Anthropic separated the agent harness, session state and execution environment.
- Letting agents use credentials without putting those credentials inside their sandboxes.
- Rebuilding the Messages API from Python to Rust with Claude—and verifying the rewrite with shadow traffic.
- Preventing model distillation while preserving the developer experience.
- Memory, “dreaming,” agent evaluations and the work still left for human engineers.
- How Anthropic’s own teams use Claude while keeping responsibility for their code and writing.
The episode opens with swyx’s look at Anthropic’s S-1: revenue per employee, compute efficiency, and the improvement and investment loops behind the business.

episodes.title: The Home Depot: How America's aging houses built the best stock of the last 45 years (Audio)
episodes.description:
The Home Depot's founding story is like an Avengers movie… if the Avengers got fired, went broke, and stacked empty paint cans ten feet high to look legitimate. After being unceremoniously fired from their previous hardware chain at ages 48 and 35, Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank took the words of their New York banker Ken Langone (who had also just accidentally caused their firings) to heart: they'd just been "kicked in the ass with a golden horseshoe.” They proceeded to author the greatest compounding story in American retail history, helped by some legendary cameos along the way from Sol Price, Jamie Dimon, and Ross Perot (to name a few). And the ending is as good as any superhero film: from its 1981 IPO to today, The Home Depot has been the single highest-returning equity in the entire US stock market — higher than Apple, Microsoft, Berkshire Hathaway, and everything else!

episodes.title: Disney: The Renaissance and the Empire (Audio)
episodes.description:
In 1984, the Walt Disney Company was worth more dead than alive. Disney Animation — the heart of Walt's famous flywheel — had stagnated for years, bleeding away talent while corporate raiders circled, salivating over offers to sell off the film library to MGM and offload the parks to hotel operators. But what followed instead was the greatest turnaround in media history under Michael Eisner and Frank Wells. Beauty and the Beast. The Lion King. Broadway. Bringing the Disney Vault home on VHS and DVD. And the greatest media acquisition of all time — ESPN.
And then... it all almost fell apart. Again. Euro Disney turned into a money pit. Boardroom and executive infighting ran rampant. Animation descended into a dumpster fire. (Remember Chicken Little? Us neither.) Comcast — Comcast!! — tried to steal the company via a hostile takeover. Out of the chaos, a new generation of Disney management emerged under Bob Iger to stage yet another epic comeback with Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm, creating the defining media empire of the 21st century…until the tech companies came along. Tune in for the ultimate Acquired thrill ride: Disney, Part II.

episodes.title: AI Software Factories
episodes.description:
“Clearly there are 100x or 1,000x engineers now. The world hasn’t adjusted.”
— Guillermo Rauch (Vercel)
Guillermo: I’ve been really pilled with this idea of software factories. You used to ship the output directly, and everything inside the company was how good is person A at shipping output B? And now what’s happening is the way that I’m judging you as an engineer is, are you producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z, right?
We used to believe, and it used to be somewhat controversial, that there’s 10X engineers. Now clearly there’s 100X or 1,000X engineers. And the world hasn’t fully adjusted to this.
@naval: I used to get flamed on Twitter for saying there are 10X engineers, because it flies in the face of so much equality philosophy that everyone’s equal. But the reality is, when you’re operating in idea domains—when you’re operating in intellectual domains and virtual digital domains—it’s not even 10X. It’s 100X or 1,000X, and it always has been.
Satoshi, Notch, the guy who invented JavaScript, the Brendan Eichs of the world. John Carmack. These are 1,000X programmers.
Not to even mention if you choose the right thing to work on versus the wrong thing to work on, that’s an infinity difference. And it could just be not necessarily even a better programmer, just one who had a better judgment of what to work on in the first place.
And now obviously it’s less controversial, because of AI leverage.

And now obviously it’s less controversial, because of AI leverage.

I demo Muse finding night nurses at $30 an hour in Montreal, show how to give it a phone number through Bland AI, and share the Marketplace and Instagram tactics I'd use. • Muse mines public Facebook groups, Marketplace, and Instagram to match buyers and sellers in any niche and city.

• Facebook groups, business pages, and IG niche pages look undervalued as Muse agents start crawling them.

• My four levels: mine the data, own the list, own the room, then build technology.
• A lean cost structure lets me charge a success fee of a few hundred dollars and keep high margins.

1. The Night Nurse Search
My wife and I recently had a baby, and our search for a night nurse led us to an agency. The agency admitted it searched Facebook groups for Miami, South Florida, and New York night nurses, and I realized Muse can do that work today. I expect a thousand-plus millionaires to come out of this era.
2. Matching Buyers and Sellers
Billions of people post needs and offers in Facebook groups, on Marketplace, and on Instagram. I pick a niche, a city, and rules for who I approve, like night nurses in Orlando, and Muse handles the structure, matching, DMs, calls, texts, and booking. The top eBay sellers made millions by finding unique products to sell, and connecting buyer and seller holds the same value here.
3. Clean Data as an Asset
Posts across these platforms vary in quality, so Muse cleans the data into Airtable, Google Sheets, or whatever I use. That list of names, needs, prices, and trust signals compounds into an asset I own and can sell, and I'll cover data brokering in a future episode. Each niche needs its own cleaning approach, starting with what my ICP wants.
4. A Phone Line and Undervalued Pages
People give Muse a dedicated number through Bland AI's Agent Line, a non-VoIP US number with talk and text that I believe costs about $15, so Muse can get a number, call me, reach out to people, and close sales. Facebook groups have about 1.8 billion monthly active users by my estimate, and with millions of Muse agents crawling them, I'd start a group, a business page like a Miami agency for night nurses, or an IG niche page now. Buying Facebook groups may also be an arbitrage, so check Facebook's terms of service first.
5. The Four Levels
Level one is mining other people's groups, Marketplace, and IG, and level two is owning a cleaned, priced, trusted list off platform. Level three is owning the room through your own Facebook group, IG niche page, or Marketplace storefront, and level four is building technology like SaaS, vertical agents, and vertical harnesses that automate the workflow end to end. Muse also works as my content hub for Instagram research, and its lean cost structure lets me charge parents a few hundred dollars where an agency team might have charged thousands.

episodes.description:
Gemini 4 Argon is LIVE, Google's most advanced AI model, try it for yourself:
In this solo episode, I share what I learned after a week with Gemini 4 Argon, Google's new frontier model. I show three places it shines: marketing with AI, physical AI, and complex engineering, with a real build for each. You'll see Argon rebuild my holding company's website, write a post in my voice, design a Shopify product customizer that exports STL files, and build a free quoting app for commercial cleaning companies. I close with six techniques that raise Argon's output quality and the Google AI plan I'd pick for building.
Timestamps

01:35 – What Gemini 4 Argon Does Well
03:09 – Rebuilding the Late Checkout Website
07:49 – Justine Moore's Apple Computer Museum
09:20 – Using Argon for writing
13:03 – Physical AI and Vibe Manufacturing
17:41 – Made-to-Order Shopify Store
19:01 – Building Boring SaaS
21:59 – Commercial Cleaning Quote App
25:12 – 6 techniques to get the most out of Argon
28:39 – Closing Thoughts
Key Points
• Argon produces premium creative work once I give it reference images and a clear direction.
• A skill built from my posts, newsletters, and videos lets Argon write in my voice.
• Argon builds Shopify product customizers that export print-ready STL files.
• Free, focused rebuilds of boring legacy SaaS put me in front of likely buyers.
• Argon gets the engineering right on prompt one, and design takes a few more rounds.
• /plan, /subagents, and /goal give me the biggest jumps in output quality.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. Where Argon Stands
After a week of testing, I see three strengths in Gemini 4 Argon: marketing with AI, physical AI, and complex engineering. Google now has a frontier-level model backed by a huge amount of data. I prefer other harnesses to Antigravity today and expect Google to catch up, and Argon also runs in Cursor and OpenCode.
2. Marketing With AI
In 2021 my team spent 40,000 hours on the Late Checkout holding company website, which cost us around $200,000, and the business has brought in more than $40 million in revenue. I asked Argon for a better version in a Mondrian style, and it added cars, movement, a world passport, sounds, and mini games like shooting a three-pointer. Justine Moore of a16z had Argon build an interactive museum of Apple computers from scraped archival photos and 50 years of specs, the kind of project that goes viral on X, TikTok, and Instagram.
3. Teaching Argon My Voice
I asked Argon to study my X posts, newsletters, and YouTube videos and turn them into a skill. It built a skill package with a core voice operating system, sentence rhythm rules, a lexicon of terms I coined, and verbatim samples and templates. Its post on marketing engineers covered micro products over PDF lead magnets and tweet-sized landing pages, signed off with "Be well, Greg," and earned a 9.2 out of 10 from me, which makes Argon probably the best frontier model for writing right now.
4. Vibe Manufacturing on Shopify Argon built me a Vibe Manufacturing Studio, an embeddable Shopify widget that shows print time, material cost, and suggested retail price, then exports a print-ready STL file. The file goes to a Bambu Lab printer, or to the Slant 3D print-on-demand API for anyone who'd rather skip owning printers. A custom espresso portafilter station shows the demand signal, since r/espresso members spend $2,500 on machines and gladly pay $49 for one.
5. Free Tools From Boring SaaS
The "SaaS is over" crowd is mostly indie hackers selling to indie hackers, and most people gladly pay for software that makes life easier. I find recurring, boring problems on G2, Capterra, Reddit, and Idea Browser, then give away a focused tool to that buyer. My test prompt asked Antigravity for a quoting app that turns a commercial cleaning company's site visit notes into a reviewed price proposal, and it nailed the engineering on prompt one.
6. Six Techniques and Pricing
I use /plan to agree on scope, /subagents to run research in parallel, /goal for higher quality, /browser to test the user journey, /learn to turn corrections into project rules, and high effort as my default after a start on medium. I tested on Google AI Ultra at $100 a month, which includes the Antigravity app, the CLI, and up to 1 million output tokens, while the $19.99 Pro plan suits text generation and web search. I close with my rule to marry the niche and date the product.

episodes.description:
I watched almost 60 minutes of Sam Altman on stage at OpenAI Dev Day 2026. Out of 20-plus launches, I pick the three or four that I think can make people billions of dollars in aggregate. I break down Dots, OpenAI's personal agent platform, plus the Decisions API, the Agents API with computer use, and Sign in with ChatGPT. I also share my four-step framework for building in this world and two business ideas I hope someone takes. If you want to build a business and make money around AI, this episode is for you.

15:04 – Idea: Analytics for Agent Discovery

Key Points
• Dots gives plugin builders a front door to 1.2 billion weekly active users.
• OpenAI is doubling down on plugins to make ChatGPT the app ecosystem for AI.
• Sign in with ChatGPT lets users bring their current plan, so a free core app with paid upsells now works.
• Workflows too niche for OpenAI to build become viable businesses.
• The strongest businesses in this world own the trigger, the action, and the feedback.
• Two open opportunities: real-world work APIs and an analytics layer for agent discovery
Numbered Section Summaries
1. The Launches Worth Your Attention
OpenAI shipped 20-plus features at Dev Day 2026, and I focus on four: Dots, the Decisions API, the Agents API, and Sign in with ChatGPT. I cover GPT 6.1 Soul, Ultrafast, Private Intelligence, and Spaces briefly at the end.
2. Dots and the Plugin Comeback
Dots is OpenAI's answer to Muse by Meta and Instinct. A user asks for help, like fixing a permit or finding a restaurant, ChatGPT understands the job, and it selects a plugin, which is essentially a mini app. By my paraphrase, Sam admitted plugins got mixed reviews before, and now he plans to make them a thing. I think billions of dollars of transactions will flow through personal agent platforms, and maybe trillions over 10 to 20 years.
3. Decisions API, OpenAI's Answer to Jev
The Decisions API is in limited preview. It focuses Luna's intelligence on user-defined questions with finite, predefined answers, so developers can classify content, route requests, or choose an agent's next action. I'm hooked on Jev, and I see UI design as an underserved use case, like finding the highest-converting app store screenshots and direct response websites.
4. Agents API and Vertical Harnesses
The Agents API now supports computer use and brings Codex's multi-agent capabilities, tool search, tool calling, and context compaction into your application. OpenAI runs the infrastructure. If you have great data, a great brand, or deep knowledge of a vertical, I would be playing with this today.
5. Sign In With ChatGPT and Free Core Apps
Users can now sign in with their ChatGPT login and use their token allowance on other websites. I compare it to Facebook login, which helped create billion-dollar companies like Yelp. People hesitate to pay $20 or $30 a month for another AI app, so I would make the core app free and charge for enterprise features, team sharing, and more data. Before, the builder paid for inference, which made a free core app hard.
6. Sell Workflows Over Tokens
Tiny AI categories are now economically viable, like an agent that cleans architectural CAD files, a researcher that monitors one scientific field, a Shopify catalog cleanup desktop app, a video tool built around one editing workflow, or a contract review tool for one type of franchise agreement. The value comes from proprietary information, a specialist workflow, access to outside systems, collaboration and auditability, a network of humans or suppliers, and a measurable business result.
7. Trigger, Decision, Action, Feedback
My framework starts with a trigger, like an invoice coming due, inventory running low, or tax time. ChatGPT decides what to do next, an application takes the action, and feedback shows whether it was approved or rejected. The strongest businesses will own the trigger, the action, and the feedback.
